reference.title: One Leg Floor Calf Raise
reference.listing: Page could not be read (blocked by the network proxy); movement taken from the exercise name and standard coaching practice
reference.note: Reference used only to identify the movement. No GymVisual media is stored here; this rig, model and animation are original.

breathing.pattern: Exhale as the heel rises, inhale as it lowers.
breathing.cadence: About 1 s up, 0.8 s pause, 1.8 s down

prescription.load: Body weight only; no external load.
prescription.progression: More reps up to about 25 full-height rises, then hold a dumbbell or stand on a step for a deeper range

cues.text: Stand on the right foot on flat floor, both hands lightly on the wall at chest height, left foot lifted behind.
Breathe out and rise as high as you can onto the ball of the right foot.
Pause at the top; stand tall, ankle straight, weight over the big toe.
Breathe in and lower the heel slowly to the floor.
Touch down lightly and repeat; then switch legs.

mistakes.fix: The hands only steady you; the calf lifts the body.
Keep the pressure through the big and second toes.
Knee straight but soft; slow lowering, pause at the top.
Rise to full height every rep; stop the set when the height drops.

kinematics.norm: Full range to as high as possible (clinical opinion); the heel-rise test counts only full-height rises (Hébert-Losier 2017)
As high as possible each rep (clinical opinion)
Straight but not locked (clinical opinion); knee angle did not change triceps surae fatigue in single-leg heel raises at 0 vs 45 degrees (Hébert-Losier 2012)
Light support with both hands on a wall for balance (clinical opinion)
About 1 s up, a short pause, about 2 s down (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual #9005, One Leg Floor Calf Raise, video (movement reference; page not readable here)

Hébert-Losier, Wessman, Alricsson & Svantesson 2017, updated reliability and normative values for the standing heel-rise test in healthy adults (Physiotherapy; doi 10.1016/j.physio.2017.03.002; PubMed 28886865)
Hébert-Losier, Schneiders, García, Sullivan & Simoneau 2012, influence of knee flexion angle and age on triceps surae muscle fatigue during heel raises (J Strength Cond Res 26(11))
Kinoshita, Maeo et al. 2023, triceps surae muscle hypertrophy is greater after standing versus seated calf-raise training (Front Physiol 14:1272106)

cautions: Stop if sharp pain, numbness or cramping occurs.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
modify: Achilles pain: two-leg raise, smaller range, slower tempo.
Poor balance: stand closer to the wall.
progressions: Single-leg calf raise holding a dumbbell.
Ball of the foot on a step for a deeper range.

muscleNotes.calves_r: Whole triceps surae with the knee straight; one leg lifts the whole body weight. Healthy adults managed a median 24 (men) and 21 (women) single-leg heel rises to fatigue (Hébert-Losier 2017).
muscleNotes.glute_med_r: Keeps the pelvis level on one leg (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.core: Holds the trunk tall over the standing foot (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.hamstrings_l: Hold the free knee bent behind (clinical opinion).

phases.label: Rise onto the balls of the feet

guides.label: Heel rises about the ball of the foot
